title: Stoichiometry
seo_title: Stoichiometry Worksheets: Mole Ratios, Limiting Reactants and Percent Yield (Chemistry)
standard_text: Use mathematical representations to support the claim that atoms, and therefore mass, are conserved during a chemical reaction.
meta_desc: Free high school chemistry worksheets on stoichiometry (NGSS HS-PS1-7): mole ratios, mole-to-mole and mass-to-mass problems, limiting reactants and percent yield. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Convert to moles, use the ratio, then convert back; the limiting reactant sets the amount.
body_html:
How to think about it

Coefficients give the mole ratio.

  • Steps: grams of A → moles of A (÷ molar mass) → moles of B (× ratio) → grams of B (× molar mass).
  • The limiting reactant runs out first; it decides how much product forms.
  • Percent yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.
Example

2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Moles of water from 3 mol O2?

3 × 2/1

Answer: 6 mol

Example

Expected 50 g, got 40 g. Percent yield?

40 ÷ 50 × 100

Answer: 80%

Common mistakes

  • Using grams directly in the mole ratio.
  • Thinking the reactant with less mass is always limiting.
  • Dividing theoretical by actual for percent yield.

faq.q: How do you do a mass-to-mass stoichiometry problem?
faq.a: Change grams of the given substance to moles, use the mole ratio from the balanced equation, then change moles of the new substance to grams.

faq.q: How do you find the limiting reactant?
faq.a: Divide the moles of each reactant by its coefficient. The smaller result is the limiting reactant.
Divide the actual yield by the theoretical yield and multiply by 100.

Why must you convert grams to moles before using the ratio?

items.q: When an acid is neutralized: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2NaOH → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the mole ratio of H<sub>2</sub>O to Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?

What is the limiting reactant?
c: the reactant with the smallest mass
the reactant that runs out first and stops the reaction

items.q: What does stoichiometry calculate?
c: the amounts of reactants and products in a reaction

items.q: What is the excess reactant?
c: the reactant left over after the reaction stops

items.q: When ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen: N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub>. What is the mole ratio of H<sub>2</sub> to NH<sub>3</sub>?
What do the coefficients in a balanced equation give?
c: the mole ratio of the substances
the mass ratio of the substances

items.q: What is theoretical yield?
c: the most product that can form, calculated from the limiting reactant

items.q: When aluminum reacts with acid: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>. How many moles of HCl react with 8 mol of Al?
items.e: 8 mol Al × (6 mol HCl ÷ 2 mol Al) = 24 mol.

When sodium reacts with chlorine: 2Na + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2NaCl. You start with 1 mol of Na and 5 mol of Cl<sub>2</sub>. How many moles of NaCl can form?

items.q: When magnesium reacts with acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>. You start with 5 mol of Mg and 1 mol of HCl. Which is the limiting reactant?
items.e: The equation needs Mg : HCl = 1 : 2; 5 mol Mg ÷ 1 = 5, 1 mol HCl ÷ 2 = 0.5. The smaller one runs out first.

items.e: The equation needs N<sub>2</sub> : H<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 3; 12 mol N<sub>2</sub> ÷ 1 = 12, 8 mol H<sub>2</sub> ÷ 3 = 2.67. The smaller one runs out first.
